---
title: "MISO manual"
subtitle: "Multivariate Inference, Similarity and Ordination for jamovi"
description: "A practical guide to the MISO jamovi module."
---

MISO brings seven multivariate analyses, implemented primarily through the
[`vegan`](https://vegandevs.github.io/vegan/) R package, into
[jamovi](https://www.jamovi.org). It is intended for ecological and biological
data, but the methods can also be useful wherever a set of numeric variables
describes samples, sites, people, or observations.

## Before you begin

Each row is a sample or observation. Use one numeric column per feature, such
as a species abundance, measurement, taxon, or biomarker. Grouping and design
variables may be categorical; integer-coded categorical variables are accepted
when set to nominal or ordinal in jamovi.

- Missing values, empty rows, and all-zero feature columns can reduce the data
  used. Read data-handling warnings when they appear.
- Transformations and dissimilarity indices change the question being asked.
  Choose them for the measurement scale and scientific design.
- Permutation p-values depend on the permutation scheme, number of
  permutations, and random seed. Record these settings when reporting results.
- An ordination represents distance structure. It is not, by itself, a test of
  statistical significance.

Choose **Analyses → MISO**, select an analysis, then assign the visible
variable targets. Result tables stay in place while an analysis is incomplete
and populate once the required inputs are valid.

## Common controls

### Feature variables

Assign the numeric variables that define multivariate similarity. Values must
be meaningful for the selected transformation and distance measure. For
example, abundance data should not contain negative values for methods that
require non-negative counts.

### Grouping and design variables

Use a **Grouping Variable** for analyses that compare groups. In PERMANOVA,
additional factors and continuous covariates extend the model, while a
**Blocking Variable** can restrict permutations within blocks. A plot may only
use a grouping factor retained in the fitted model; MISO explains when a
requested display factor cannot be used.

### Transformation, distance, and plots

MISO offers standard transformations and several dissimilarity indices.
Bray-Curtis is common for non-negative abundance data, whereas Euclidean
distance is often appropriate after transformations that make it meaningful.
Plot backgrounds are transparent. Centroids, hulls, ellipses, and
site-centroid connections change a visual layer, not the fitted result.

## PERMANOVA

**PERMANOVA** tests whether multivariate group locations differ using
permutations (`vegan::adonis2`). Assign feature variables and one categorical
grouping variable. You can add factors, covariates, model interactions, and a
blocking variable.

Read **PERMANOVA Results** as an analysis-of-variance table: **Pseudo-F**
compares separation among model terms with within-group variation, **R²** is
the variation associated with a term, and **Permutation p** is the evidence
against the null model. The result note identifies the distance,
transformation, permutation restriction, test type, and blocking status.
Optional pairwise results appear only when requested. The companion PCoA is a
visual aid to the fitted resemblance structure, not another test.

## ANOSIM

**ANOSIM** compares ranked between-group and within-group dissimilarities
(`vegan::anosim`). Assign feature variables and a grouping variable. The
global statistic is closer to 1 when between-group dissimilarities tend to
exceed within-group dissimilarities; its permutation p-value assesses that
pattern under the selected scheme. The ranked-dissimilarity plot is diagnostic,
not a separate significance test.

## PERMDISP

**PERMDISP** tests whether groups differ in multivariate dispersion
(`vegan::betadisper`). Use it alongside PERMANOVA when group differences could
be caused by unequal dispersion rather than location. The dispersion table
reports the permutation test; the distance-to-centre diagnostic shows the
individual distances behind it. An optional ordination is for inspection.

## nMDS

**nMDS** produces a non-metric multidimensional scaling ordination
(`vegan::metaMDS`). Assign feature variables and, optionally, a grouping
variable and environmental variables. Stress summarises how well the plotted
configuration represents ranked dissimilarities: lower stress is usually
preferable, but suitability depends on the data and should be judged with the
Shepard diagram and substantive knowledge.

**Group point styling** applies colour and shape by group. Hulls, ellipses,
spiders, environmental vectors, and feature scores are overlays that help
describe the ordination. Do not read apparent separation as a formal test
without an appropriate inferential analysis.

## Cluster analysis

**Cluster analysis** builds a hierarchical dendrogram from the chosen
dissimilarity matrix (`vegan::vegdist` and `stats::hclust`). It is descriptive:
use it to explore similarity structure, not to claim a tested group effect.
MISO uses group-average linkage. You can choose optional sample labels. Turn on **Cluster
definition** to add a cut by number of clusters or dissimilarity height; MISO
then reports cluster membership. The plot and dendrogram structure remain
available without a definition.

## SIMPER

**SIMPER** decomposes Bray-Curtis dissimilarity into feature contributions
(`vegan::simper`). Assign feature variables and a grouping variable, then read
the table as a descriptive ranking of features contributing to group contrasts.
It is sensitive to dispersion and correlated features, so it is not a
confirmatory feature-selection method.

Use the cumulative-contribution threshold to focus the table. Contribution
plots and the optional heatmap are descriptive. **Permutation contribution
assessment** adds an exploratory assessment using the selected permutations,
p-value adjustment, and seed; interpret it alongside the study design and
global multivariate analysis.

## PCoA

**PCoA** displays distance structure with principal coordinates
(`vegan::wcmdscale`). Assign feature variables and optionally a grouping
variable. Eigenvalues and explained percentages describe the axes. Negative
eigenvalues can occur for non-Euclidean distances; use an additive correction,
if appropriate, and report that decision.

Group centroids and **Site-centroid connections** are optional visual layers.
They require a grouping variable and do not alter the coordinates or
eigenvalues. Coordinate and centroid tables make plotted values available for
checking and reporting.

## Reporting and citation

State the feature set, transformation, dissimilarity index, permutation design,
number of permutations, random seed, and any multiple-comparison adjustment.
Report effect sizes as well as p-values, and distinguish exploratory plots from
formal inferential results. MISO cites `vegan` and the core method references
in its output: Anderson (2001) for PERMANOVA, Anderson (2006) for PERMDISP,
and Clarke (1993) for ANOSIM and SIMPER.

## Limitations and support

MISO is a convenient jamovi interface, not a replacement for checking model
assumptions, study design, and the underlying R methods. For analyses or
options not offered here, use `vegan` directly. If a result is surprising,
inspect the warnings, table notes, settings, and data before interpreting it.
